```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

# Load the prepared dataset
data <- read_csv("../data/processed/final_data.csv")

# Check data structure
glimpse(data)

# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(data))
```

```{r}
# Count affected countries by year
conflict_by_year <- data |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    affected_countries = sum(armed_conflict == 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(conflict_by_year)

#Code for the time-trend analysis
ggplot(conflict_by_year,
       aes(x = year, y = affected_countries)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2019, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Countries Experiencing Armed Conflict",
    subtitle = "2000–2019",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Countries"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Highest number of affected countries
conflict_by_year |>
  slice_max(affected_countries, n = 1)

# Lowest number of affected countries
conflict_by_year |>
  slice_min(affected_countries, n = 1)
```
### Exploratory Data Analysis: Armed Conflict
I explored how the number of countries experiencing armed conflict changed from 2000 to 2019. The dataset contains observations from 186 countries over 20 years. I first checked for missing values and found that the armed conflict indicator had no missing observations. Then, I grouped the data by year and calculated the number of countries experiencing armed conflict each year. I used a line plot to visualize the changes over time.

The results showed that the number of affected countries fluctuated throughout the study period. The highest number was recorded in 2017, with 49 countries, while the lowest was in 2011, with 28 countries. There was a noticeable increase between 2015 and 2017, followed by a decrease in 2018. Overall, the results do not suggest a consistent increasing or decreasing trend over the entire period.

```{r}
#Exploring the relationship between armed conflict and under-five mortality
mortality_data <- data |>
  filter(!is.na(under5_mortality)) |>
  mutate(
    conflict_status = factor(
      armed_conflict,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No Conflict", "Conflict")
    )
  )

ggplot(mortality_data,
       aes(x = conflict_status, y = under5_mortality,
           fill = conflict_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Under-Five Mortality by Armed Conflict Status",
    subtitle = "2000–2019",
    x = "Armed Conflict Status",
    y = "Under-Five Mortality (per 1,000 live births)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

mortality_by_year <- mortality_data |>
  group_by(year, conflict_status) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mortality = mean(under5_mortality),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(mortality_by_year,
       aes(x = year,
           y = mean_mortality,
           color = conflict_status)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Under-Five Mortality by Conflict Status",
    subtitle = "2000–2019",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Under-Five Mortality (per 1,000)",
    color = "Conflict Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### Exploring the Relationship Between Armed Conflict and Under-Five Mortality
As an extension of the time-trend analysis, I explored the relationship between armed conflict and under-five mortality from 2000 to 2019. I grouped the observations by armed conflict status and calculated descriptive statistics for under-five mortality. The mean mortality rate was approximately 66.86 per 1,000 live births for country-years experiencing armed conflict, compared with 34.31 for those without conflict. I used a boxplot to compare the distributions and a line plot to examine how mortality rates changed over time.

The results showed that under-five mortality was consistently higher in the conflict group throughout the study period. Both groups experienced declining mortality rates over time, but the difference between them remained substantial. These findings suggest an association between armed conflict and higher under-five mortality. However, further analysis would be necessary to account for other factors that may influence mortality rates.
